https://www.koco.com/article/venice-film.text: August can be a dreary month for Hollywood glamour, but the Venice Film Festival is on the horizon to kick off the busy fall film festival season in style. There will be plenty of stars gracing the red carpets when the 83rd edition of the festival kicks off Wednesday on the Lido: Noel and Liam Gallagher, Robert Pattinson, Rooney Mara, George Clooney and Penélope Cruz are among those expected to attend. Some of the films may even become Oscar nominees. But the mood feels a little different this year. There will always be a spotlight for the Hollywood contingent and the awards hopefuls posing on boats and docks in designer duds. Yet, in a lineup featuring Pattinson as "To Catch a Predator" host Chris Hansen, Dakota Johnson as Marilyn Monroe, Guy Pearce as Rupert Murdoch and Clooney as, well, himself (he's getting a lifetime achievement award, as is Ellen Burstyn), it's possible that much of the attention will be on a man who (probably) won't be there: Elon Musk. Docs feature Musk, Russia and Gaza Alex Gibney's nearly four-hour documentary about the world's richest man has been in the works for almost four years. The Oscar-winner wasn't sure about taking it on at first, but a good friend convinced him it would be a worthy portrait of 21st-century power — and this was before the 2024 presidential campaign and DOGE. When the documentary was announced, Musk called it a "hit piece" on social media. Gibney replied, "How would you know?" In fact, Gibney told The Associated Press he started off as a kind of admirer — as well as a Tesla owner — and sincerely wanted to talk to Musk for the film. "Ultimately, he didn't want to talk to me," Gibney said. "But then you start, you know, digging into the facts and you follow them where they lead. And where they led, for me, was to a place that upended the myth, I would say, of Elon Musk as a kind of modern Leonardo da Vinci … I think that the news in this film is that Musk isn't an inventor. He's a confidence man." The filmmakers talked to hundreds of people on and off the record to compile a sweeping picture of the Tesla and SpaceX CEO who, Gibney said, is not dissimilar to the guys at Enron or Elizabeth Holmes. He was most surprised by how many people seemed to be afraid to be on camera talking about Musk — even his admirers wanted permission first. "I thought, wow, for such a big and powerful person, that seems awfully weak," Gibney said. But while it's a "dark and dangerous topic," Gibney said, the film is also a "fun ride." The same could be said of "My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile," in which Julia Loktev continues her sprawling portrait of independent Russian journalists after the invasion of Ukraine. "You see this group of young, very young journalists who've just fled their country, like, on a few hours' notice. They had the choice of, you know, stop reporting the truth about the war, which didn't seem like a choice at all, or go to prison, or leave the country so they can keep telling the truth," Loktev said. "It was a question of how long do you keep following? Because this takes place over four years. And over that time, exile becomes, of course, indefinite." Similar to the first film, Part II runs nearly six hours. But, she said, "I hear it goes by easy." The conflict in Gaza will also take center stage in the documentary "NAZA," a late addition to the competition, from two of the filmmakers behind the Oscar-winning "No Other Land." Unlike last year, no large-scale protests are planned, but the group Venice4Palestine did call on the festival to "suspend all agreements with entities and institutions linked to the Israeli government." It also asked that the Palestinian flag be flown throughout. Hollywood eyes awards in Venice Part of the intrigue of Venice is how it might play into the Oscar race — it's usually good for a best picture nominee or two. Martin McDonagh's "Wild Horse Nine," starring John Malkovich and Sam Rockwell as 1970s CIA agents, seems like a promising candidate after his last two films debuted at Venice and went on to nominations. "The Father" filmmaker Florian Zeller returns with "Bunker," a psychological thriller with Cruz and Javier Bardem. Danny Boyle looks at a turning point in tabloid media in "Ink." And there's much curiosity around Lance Oppenheim's "Primetime," for Pattinson's performance and for its examination of reality television culture in the early 2000s. Japanese filmmaker Hirokazu Kore-eda is also debuting "Look Back," about two small-town girls who aspire to be manga artists. And Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong examines themes of labor and freedom through two married couples in "Possible Love." This is also a year in which big Hollywood hasn't needed the sheen of the international film festival. Cannes was bereft of a big blockbuster, and the industry went on to have one of its highest-earning summers ever. The reigning best picture winner, "One Battle After Another," skipped festivals entirely. Venice might have more Hollywood films than Cannes did, but following several years in which fates might have been prematurely decided for both would-be contenders, like "After the Hunt" and "The Smashing Machine," and blockbusters like "Joker: Folie à Deux," it too seems a bit more muted — at least on paper. Venice fails in its pledge to women And then there is the subject of women, specifically those behind the camera. There is only one in the main competition: Danish-Egyptian director May El-Toukhy. The same thing happened in 2018, prompting the festival that year to sign a pledge to have at least half of the films in competition be directed by women by 2020, which they have yet to achieve. Adding more insult to injury is the fact that Maggie Gyllenhaal, whose first film "The Lost Daughter" won Venice's best screenplay prize in 2021, is presiding over a jury which includes Kaouther Ben Hania, whose film "The Voice of Hind Rajab" won the Silver Lion last year when there were six female-directed films in the competition. Only seven women have won the Golden Lion, including Laura Poitras with "All the Beauty and the Bloodshed," who is returning this year with a short film she co-directed with Rachel Lauren Mueller about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Minneapolis. "They're Here" is part of the Venice Open section, which also includes Gyllenhaal's Marilyn Monroe short "Flesh Impact." Outside of the main competition, there are also documentaries from Loktev, Barbara Kopple and Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi. There are several others in the Horizons sections as well, including a short from Saoirse Ronan. Opening Venice Days on Wednesday is Hungarian filmmaker Lili Horvát's English-language debut, "My Notes on Mars," about a couple — Rupert Friend and Mackenzie Davis — whose marriage is in trouble when the wife, a scientist, mysteriously disappears and then reappears the day of her memorial service. "The story argues for great love," Horvát said. "Yet it shows the eternal limits of knowing the person we are in love with." Venice Days is an independent sidebar in which more than half the selections are by women, including several high-profile shorts from filmmakers like Mona Fastvold and Claire Denis. "It's good to be in a progressive section," Horvát said.

https://english.news.cn/20260928/6488ff5.text: World Insights: Polish-Ukrainian solidarity frays amid growing differences Source: Xinhua Editor: huaxia 2026-09-28 00:11:45 WARSAW, Sept. 27 (Xinhua) -- A knife attack by a Ukrainian national at a monastery in southeastern Poland has brought renewed attention to the ever more complicated relationship between the two neighbors. A 31-year-old Ukrainian citizen reportedly killed a priest and injured four other people at a Benedictine monastery in Jaroslaw on Thursday. A court on Saturday ordered him held in pretrial detention for three months, and the motive for the attack remained unclear. The incident has quickly stirred political reactions in Poland. Members and supporters of National Movement, a Polish right-wing nationalist party, gathered outside the monastery, while some politicians called for tighter controls on migrants, including Ukrainians. Poland remains a major supporter of Ukraine and a key logistical hub for assistance, but the strong solidarity with Ukraine forged in the early days of the Russia-Ukraine conflict is giving way to the harder politics of a long-term relationship, as migration, competing economic interests and historical grievances return to the fore. FROM SOLIDARITY TO FATIGUE When the Russia-Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022, Poland became a major destination for Ukrainians fleeing the fighting. The country introduced special measures giving eligible Ukrainians access to employment, public healthcare and social benefits. Public support was overwhelming. According to Poland's Public Opinion Research Center (CBOS), 94 percent of respondents supported accepting Ukrainian refugees from conflict-affected areas in early 2022. Four years on, however, what began as temporary refuge has evolved into a longer-term challenge of migration and integration, adding to friction between Poles and Ukrainians. According to Eurostat, more than 953,000 people displaced from Ukraine remained under temporary protection in Poland at the end of July, the second-largest number in the European Union (EU) after Germany. Public attitudes have shifted markedly. A CBOS survey released in July showed that 52 percent of respondents opposed accepting Ukrainian refugees, the first time since the agency began tracking the issue that opponents outnumbered supporters. The change in public attitudes has been accompanied by signs of growing hostility toward Ukrainians. Polish police received 180 reports of suspected hate crimes targeting Ukrainian citizens in the first half of 2026, up more than 30 percent from the same period a year earlier, according to police data. POLITICAL FRICTIONS GROW Political tensions have also grown as Ukraine-related issues become increasingly intertwined with domestic politics in Poland and historical disputes resurface between the two countries. Polish President Karol Nawrocki last year vetoed legislation extending assistance measures for Ukrainian citizens, arguing that the country's 800-zloty (210 U.S. dollars) monthly child benefit should be available only to Ukrainians who work in Poland. The employment requirement took effect in February, as Poland began scaling back some of the special arrangements for Ukrainians. Special access to public healthcare was largely phased out in March, and state-funded collective accommodation was restricted mainly to specified vulnerable groups. Historical disputes have further fueled friction between the two countries, particularly over the Volhynia massacres during World War II and the legacy of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). In late May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky approved the naming of a Ukrainian military unit after the UPA. Nawrocki responded by revoking the Order of the White Eagle, Poland's highest state decoration, which was awarded to Zelensky in 2023, calling the Ukrainian move "outrageous, incomprehensible and deeply disappointing." Zelensky returned the decoration the following day. Polish geopolitical analyst Malwina Talik noted that although the two presidents' decisions had triggered a deep diplomatic crisis, both moves enjoyed broad support in their respective countries. She said the dispute was rooted in divergent historical memories of the UPA in Poland and Ukraine, making it particularly difficult to resolve. DIVERGING INTERESTS A study published by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace said security remains the area where Polish and Ukrainian strategic interests are most closely aligned, but appears to be the "lowest common denominator" in their relationship rather than the foundation for a comprehensive partnership. Differences have emerged even over security. Edwin Bendyk, president of Poland's Stefan Batory Foundation, has highlighted a growing asymmetry between the two countries: while the conflict remains an existential issue for Ukrainians, Poles are primarily concerned with avoiding direct confrontation. The Carnegie study, citing interviews with Polish officials, said some viewed Ukraine as a buffer state rather than a full-fledged ally integrated with Europe. It also pointed to Warsaw's cautious approach to the Coalition of the Willing, with Poland ruling out sending troops to Ukraine. Economic relations reveal another limit to the partnership. Disputes over Ukrainian agricultural exports led Poland to restrict some imports and sparked border protests, while tensions persist over increasing Ukrainian grain transit through Poland. The Carnegie study said the issue had grown from an economic concern into an electoral issue before "spiraling into a serious bilateral crisis." The stakes extend beyond bilateral relations, with tensions between Poland and Ukraine carrying potential implications for Ukraine's accession to the EU, according to Talik. ■

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Booking.com said it was engaging constructively with the commission. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters View image in fullscreen Booking.com said it was engaging constructively with the commission. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters European Union Booking.com under investigation by EU regulators over fake listings and scams European Commission calls accommodation website’s approach to fraudulent listings and phishing scams as ‘absolutely substandard’ Jennifer Rankin Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.01 EDT Last modified on Wed 21 Oct 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google EU regulators have opened an investigation into Booking.com, alleging that the accommodation website has not done enough to protect consumers from fake listings and scams. The European Commission , which regulates the world’s biggest tech companies operating in the EU, said Booking.com may have breached the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) with its “absolutely substandard” approach to tackling fraudulent listings and phishing scams, where criminals impersonate a third party to trick people to hand over money. A commission official said Booking.com should be carrying out risk assessments and acting to prevent fraud as required under the DSA. “We feel that what they have done is absolutely substandard,” said the official. “Although they take measures, they could go much further and they could have much more solid systems to prevent fraud.” EU officials will also investigate whether Booking.com has breached advertising transparency rules, by potentially not making clear to users that some accommodation providers had paid to make their business more visible on the website. View image in fullscreen Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission’s executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy. Photograph: Olivier Matthys/EPA Under the EU’s DSA, which aims to protect people from harmful and illegal internet content, a company could be fined 6% of its worldwide annual turnover. The commission said that opening the investigation did not prejudge the outcome. Booking.com, which is headquartered in Amsterdam and claims to have 28m accommodation listings, said it was engaging constructively with the commission. “Security, trust and the protection of personal information are top priorities at Booking.com,” a company spokesperson said. “We remain committed to working with relevant governments, regulators, law enforcement and industry partners to ‌combat cybercrime and online fraud, and protect travellers and partners.” The investigation comes after researchers at the UK consumer group Which? exposed security lapses at Booking.com when they used the site to set up – and accept payment for – a fake offer to stay at 10 Downing Street. EU officials are investigating similar scams, with less high-profile addresses, where consumers thought they had booked a stay, only to find on arrival at a property that it had been fraudulently listed on Booking.com. Officials are also assessing a second category of scams, dubbed “reservation hijacks” where scammers use hacked data to impersonate an accommodation provider. Criminals send WhatsApp messages and have even used Booking.com’s own platform to request payments from Booking.com’s customers, supposedly to secure a stay. Cases seen by Guardian Money in 2025 involved the theft of several hundred pounds. EU officials will examine whether the company has sufficient safeguards to prevent data from being misused. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion The Dutch consumer association Consumentenbond said it had received 200 reports of scams costing people €65,000 that involved Booking.com in 2025, up from 89 reports worth €25,000 the previous year. These cases were “just the tip of the iceberg”, it said, as many victims would not report to its fraud helpdesk. Booking.com told the BBC in 2024 it had seen a 500 to 900% increase in scams in the previous 18 months, driven by generative AI tools that enable fraudsters to create very realistic-looking fake emails and internet booking links. Agustín Reyna, director general of the pan-European consumer group BEUC, said: “It is positive to see the European Commission investigating Booking.com for failing to meet EU digital rules. This is a systemic problem.” Henna Virkkunen, the commission’s lead official on tech policy, said: “Europeans should be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed. The Digital Services Act sets clear responsibilities on platforms to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes those responsibilities seriously.” Explore more on these topics European Union Europe European Commission Internet safety Scams Cybercrime Identity fraud news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.politico.eu/article/ngo-brus.text: Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’ links to the agro-chemical giant Agrofert represent a conflict of interest and EU subsidies could be withheld as a result, according to an NGO’s account of a letter it received from the European Commission. Ahead of his return to power in December 2025, Babiš placed Agrofert in a trust fund in an effort to preserve its eligibility for EU farm cash. However, that appears not to have convinced Brussels. Transparency International Czechia quotes a letter from DG AGRI Director-General Elisabeth Werner, confirming that “the Commission concluded that Mr Babiš’ situation constitutes a conflict of interest” under EU financial regulations. The trust fund and “measures currently being implemented and notified to the Commission are insufficient” to resolve it, she adds, according to the watchdog NGO, which said it was not allowed to publish the letter. Advertisement Advertisement Babiš has been under renewed scrutiny over Agrofert — a large agro-chemical conglomerate and a major recipient of EU funds — as well as other companies since his return to power last year. Babiš placed the company in a trust fund in a bid to avoid a conflict of interest, but the arrangement has raised questions from both the Commission and the Czech opposition , partly because his children would benefit from it after his death. Babiš has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. “I don’t own Agrofert, I never will again and I don’t benefit from it in any way. I don’t know what else I’m supposed to do,” he told Czech media last month. “Apparently, even if I shot myself, it still wouldn’t be enough.” Babiš’ office did not immediately reply to POLITICO’s request for comment about the contents of the letter. Werner warned in the letter that Brussels would take all necessary steps to protect EU funds, “including the possible interruption of payment deadlines, suspension of payments or application of financial corrections,” according to TI Czechia. TI Czechia Executive Director David Kotora told POLITICO that he received the letter in September. A follow-up letter from Werner dated Oct. 5 gives the NGO permission to share the contents of the letter without publishing it. The conflict-of-interest dispute echoes Babiš’ first term as prime minister, when a Commission audit found he still controlled Agrofert. That left Czech taxpayers to foot the bill for EU subsidies deemed to be erroneously paid. History could now repeat itself as Brussels last month froze €3.18 million in reimbursements to the Czech state for farm subsidies paid out to Agrofert. That followed its earlier May decision that it would not reimburse any paid-out subsidies until doubts about his involvement in the business could be put to rest. Commission spokesperson Louise Bogey confirmed it had sent a letter to TI Czechia in September, but would not comment on its content. However, she pointed to her remarks at a Sept. 8 midday briefing , during which she said Babiš was in a “potential conflict of interest” and that “the Commission considers the trust fund set up by Mr. Babiš does not sufficiently mitigate this situation.” Czechia’s agricultural paying agency, which earlier decided that the conglomerate is eligible for EU subsidies despite the Commission’s warning, said Tuesday it had sent clarifications to the Commission this week. Agrofert spokesperson Pavel Heřmanský said neither Agrofert nor any of its subsidiaries were involved in the communication between the Commission and Czech authorities. “The cited letter from DG AGRI expresses the opinion of one of the European Commission’s departments. It does not constitute an official position of the European Commission,” said Heřmanský in a statement, adding that “only the Court of Justice of the European Union can provide a binding interpretation of European Union law.” He added: “We remain convinced that we have received and continue to receive subsidies in compliance with both Czech and European law.”
